# Incident Report — MTA 2026-02-28 Traffic Analysis Exercise

**Evidence:** `2026-02-28-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (15,512 frames). No IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence folder — findings below are derived directly from packet analysis via tshark.

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.2.28.88** |
| MAC address | **00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad** (Intel NIC) |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR** |
| AD domain | EASYAS123 (FQDN `easyas123.tech`), DC at 10.2.28.2 (`easyas123-dc.easyas123.tech`) |
| Logged-in user | **brolf** (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REP, realm `EASYAS123.TECH`) |
| OS / browser fingerprint | Windows NT 10.0, x64; Chrome/145.0.0.0 (Edg/145.0.0.0) — from HTTP User-Agent on legitimate traffic |

Host identity was corroborated across three independent sources: DHCP (`bootp.option.hostname = DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR`), NetBIOS Name Service registrations (workstation + domain `EASYAS123`), and Kerberos ticket exchanges with the DC.

## 2. Malware Family

**NetSupport RAT** (malicious use of the NetSupport Manager remote-control client), aka NetSupport Manager RAT.

**Attribution: signature-confirmed**, not behavioral. Two hard artifacts prove it:
- HTTP `User-Agent: NetSupport Manager/1.3` on every outbound request to the C2.
- The literal NetSupport client-server protocol tokens observed in the POST bodies to `/fakeurl.htm`:
  - `CMD=POLL\nINFO=1\nACK=1\n` (heartbeat/poll)
  - `CMD=ENCD\nES=1\nDATA=<hex-encoded encrypted blob>\n` (encrypted command/control channel)

This is the well-documented NetSupport RAT check-in format. All traffic to the C2 is plain HTTP (no TLS handshake was found on this stream) carried over TCP/443, a known trick this family uses to blend in with expected "HTTPS" port traffic while evading TLS inspection.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

**C2 endpoint**
- `45.131.214.85:443` (TCP, plaintext HTTP — not TLS)

**Malicious domain**
- `vadusa.xyz` → resolved by DNS to `45.131.214.85`

**Malicious URL**
- `http://45.131.214.85/fakeurl.htm` (Host header sent as the raw IP; same path pattern would resolve identically via `vadusa.xyz`)

**Traffic pattern / session details**
- First beacon: frame 2569, 2026-02-28 23:55:51 (+0400) — occurs immediately (≈0.1s) after the DNS resolution of `vadusa.xyz`, and directly follows a burst of TLS traffic to `www.fmcsa.dot.gov` (23.64.147.24) seconds earlier. This timing is consistent with a fake/lure page as the infection trigger, but the pcap alone does not capture the script or executable that initiated it, so I can't confirm that page as the delivery vector — only the timing correlation.
- 550 total HTTP transactions (276 client POSTs / 274 server responses) between 10.2.28.88:51912 and 45.131.214.85:443.
- Traffic persisted for the full remainder of the capture, ending at 2026-03-01 04:16:28 (+0400) — roughly 4.3 hours of continuous beaconing.

**Transferred files / hashes**
- **None recoverable.** After the initial `CMD=POLL` handshake, all C2 traffic is wrapped in NetSupport's proprietary encryption (`CMD=ENCD` / `ES=1` / `DATA=<encrypted>`), so no file names, file transfers, or hashes are visible in cleartext anywhere in this capture. No executable payload delivery to the host was observed in the pcap either — the RAT client was already present and beaconing when capture data becomes relevant to the infection.

**Ruled out as false positives** (legitimate traffic, confirmed via correct SNI/hostname and standard Microsoft/Adobe infrastructure): Windows Update (`ctldl.windowsupdate.com`, BITS delivery via `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com`), Defender definition updates, OCSP/DigiCert cert checks, `www.msftconnecttest.com` (NCSI), and various `*.microsoft.com`/`*.msn.com`/Adobe/Bing telemetry endpoints.

## Summary

Windows workstation **DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR** (10.2.28.88, MAC 00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad), logged on as domain user **brolf** in the `EASYAS123.TECH` AD environment, is compromised with **NetSupport RAT**, signature-confirmed by the `NetSupport Manager/1.3` user-agent and `CMD=POLL`/`CMD=ENCD` protocol strings. The malware beacons continuously to **45.131.214.85:443** (domain **vadusa.xyz**) via plaintext HTTP over port 443, POSTing to **`/fakeurl.htm`**, for over 4 hours in the capture. No file names or hashes could be extracted since the C2 payload channel is encrypted and no dropper transfer appears in this pcap.
